仅凭已有知识，我可以给出如下回答（未检索，可能有版本或参数细节不准确）：

**分析流程（Nsight Compute, ncu）**
1. 用 `ncu --set full ./app` 或 `ncu --section MemoryWorkloadAnalysis --section Occupancy ./app` 采集 kernel 数据；GUI 端用 `ncu-ui` 打开报告。
2. 先看 SpeedOfLight (SOL) 段：判断是 memory-bound 还是 compute-bound；Memory Throughput 高而 SM 低 → 访存受限。
3. Memory Workload Analysis：检查 L1/L2 命中率、全局/共享内存事务。
4. Occupancy 段：查看 Achieved Occupancy vs Theoretical Occupancy，以及限制因素（register / shared memory / block size），配合 "Occupancy Calculator" 图表（ncu GUI 中有 CUDA Occupancy Calculator 导入 .h 或用 launch stats）。
5. 优化方向：
   - **Memory coalescing**：确保 warp 内线程访问连续地址；看 `l1tex__t_sectors_per_request` 指标，sectors/request 高说明未合并；调整数据布局 AoS→SoA、让 threadIdx.x 对应连续地址。
   - **Shared memory**：用 `__shared__` 做数据复用/tile（如矩阵乘 stencil）；注意 `--maxrregcount` 或 `cudaFuncAttributePreferredSharedMemoryCarveout` 调整 carveout。
   - **Bank conflict**：共享内存按 32 个 bank（每 bank 4 字节），同 warp 多线程访问同 bank 不同地址会串行化；看 `l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu_mem_shared` 指标；用 padding（如 `tile[N][N+1]`）消除。
   - **Occupancy**：用 CUDA Occupancy Calculator（`cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` API 或 CUDA 安装目录下的 Excel 表）计算；通过减少每线程寄存器（`__launch_bounds__`）、调整 block size（128–256）、控制 shared memory 用量提升理论 occupancy；但 memory-bound kernel 未必需要很高 occupancy，关键是足够的内存级并行（ILP/TLP）。

**不确定处**
- 当前最新 ncu 版本号、确切的 CLI section 名（如 `LaunchStats`、`SchedulerStats`）和新指标命名（各代架构指标前缀可能不同，如 `l1tex__` vs `sm__`）可能有版本差异。
- ncu 与具体 GPU 架构（Hopper/Blackwell）的兼容版本对应关系需查官方 release notes。
- `ncu` 的 `--set roofline`、source-level analysis（`--set full` + `-lineinfo`）等参数细节需核对官方文档。

# Nsight Compute Profiling Guide — Extracted Information

> **⚠️ Truncation Notice:** The provided content was **truncated** at section **2.4.2 "Launch Metrics"** (marked `[content truncated]`). Information about guided analysis rules is largely absent, and detailed metric tables from the Metrics Reference (2.4.x) onward were not included in the source.

---

## 1. How to Profile CUDA Kernels

**Execution model:** The Nsight Compute frontend (UI or CLI) launches the application on the target system and injects measurement libraries into the process to intercept CUDA user-mode driver communication and collect GPU performance metrics per kernel launch.

**Key CLI options for controlling collection:**
| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `--set full` | Collect the full set of sections |
| `--section <name>` | Collect specific section(s) |
| `--metrics <names>` | Collect specific metrics |
| `--list-sets` | List available section sets |
| `--list-sections` | List available sections |
| `--query-metrics` | Query available metrics |
| `--query-metrics-mode suffix` | Show metric sub-metric suffixes |
| `--chip <name>` (e.g., `--chip ga100`) | Query metrics for a specific chip |
| `--launch-count 1` | Limit to one launch |
| `--kill yes` | Terminate app after profiling |
| `--clock-control none` | Disable clock locking |
| `--replay-mode application` | Use application replay |
| `--cache-control none` | Disable cache flushing |
| `--app-replay-match` | Select kernel matching strategy (default: *grid* = kernel name + grid size) |

**Default behavior:** If no `--set`, `--section`, or `--metrics` is passed, the **`basic`** set is collected (high-level utilization + static launch/occupancy data, no replay needed).

**Replay modes** (needed because not all metrics fit in one pass):
- **Kernel Replay** — saves/restores GPU memory between passes; skipped if only one pass is needed
- **Application Replay** — re-runs the entire app; no memory save/restore; supports host-dependent kernels; requires deterministic app behavior
- **Range Replay** — captures/replays a range of CUDA API calls + kernels (defined via `cu(da)ProfilerStart/Stop` or NVTX via `--nvtx --nvtx-include <expression>`); avoids kernel serialization
- **Application Range Replay** — range-based, but re-runs whole app; limitation: no instruction-level SASS data for JIT-compiled kernels

**Example commands from the doc:**
```
ncu --query-metrics-mode suffix --metrics sm__inst_executed --chip ga100
ncu --query-metrics-mode suffix --metrics smsp__average_warp_latency --chip ga100
ncu --query-metrics-mode suffix --metrics sm__throughput --chip ga100
```

---

## 2. SpeedOfLight Section

- **Identifier:** `SpeedOfLight`
- **Display Name:** GPU Speed Of Light Throughput
- **Description (verbatim):** *"High-level overview of the throughput for compute and memory resources of the GPU. For each unit, the throughput reports the achieved percentage of utilization with respect to the theoretical maximum. Breakdowns show the throughput for each individual sub-metric of Compute and Memory to clearly identify the highest contributor."*

**Extension sections (roofline charts):**
| Identifier | Display Name |
|---|---|
| `SpeedOfLight_RooflineChart` | GPU Speed Of Light Roofline Chart (Overview) |
| `SpeedOfLight_HierarchicalSingleRooflineChart` | Hierarchical Roofline Chart (Single Precision) |
| `SpeedOfLight_HierarchicalDoubleRooflineChart` | Hierarchical Roofline Chart (Double Precision) |
| `SpeedOfLight_HierarchicalHalfRooflineChart` | Hierarchical Roofline Chart (Half Precision) |
| `SpeedOfLight_HierarchicalTensorRooflineChart` | Hierarchical Roofline Chart (Tensor Core) |

---

## 3. Memory Workload Analysis Section

- **Identifier:** `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis`
- **Description (verbatim):** *"Detailed analysis of the memory resources of the GPU. Memory can become a limiting factor for the overall kernel performance when fully utilizing the involved hardware units (**Mem Busy**), exhausting the available communication bandwidth between those units (**Max Bandwidth**), or by reaching the maximum throughput of issuing memory instructions (**Mem Pipes Busy**)."*

**Extension sections:**
- `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis_Chart` — detailed chart of memory units
- `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis_Tables` — detailed tables per memory unit

**Also reported here:** L1/L2 cache hit/miss rates, data transfers, texture/surface memory info, and detailed memory metrics.

**Supporting memory model details:**
- **Global memory** — 49-bit virtual address space; accessed through SM L1 and GPU L2 caches
- **Local memory** — thread-private; resides in device memory; caused by register spilling, non-constant-indexed arrays, large structures. Best practices given: prefer registers, use shared memory, increase registers via `__maxnreg__` / `__launch_bounds__`, increase L1 via `cudaFuncSetCacheConfig`, or compile with `-Xptxas –def-load-cache=cg`
- **L1/L2 relationship** — L1TEX handles global/local/shared/texture/surface; L2 sits between on-chip clients and framebuffer, handles compression and global atomics

---

## 4. Occupancy Section

- **Identifier:** `Occupancy`
- **Description (verbatim):** *"Occupancy is the ratio of the number of active warps per multiprocessor to the maximum number of possible active warps... Higher occupancy does not always result in higher performance, however, low occupancy always reduces the ability to hide latencies, resulting in overall performance degradation. Large discrepancies between the theoretical and the achieved occupancy during execution typically indicates highly imbalanced workloads."*

**Related concepts:** CTA occupancy is limited by threads, registers, shared memory, and hardware barriers. The **CUDA Occupancy Calculator** computes `launch__occupancy_per_*` metrics.

---

## 5. Launch Statistics Section

- **Identifier:** `LaunchStats`
- **Description (verbatim):** *"Summary of the configuration used to launch the kernel. The launch configuration defines the size of the kernel grid, the division of the grid into blocks, and the GPU resources needed to execute the kernel. Choosing an efficient launch configuration maximizes device utilization."*

**Key facts:**
- Shows the kernel's **register usage**
- `launch__*` metrics are collected per kernel launch **without requiring an extra replay pass**
- For range-based results, `launch__*` metrics are instanced per launch, **except** `launch__uses_*`, `launch__graph_*`, and `launch__occupancy_per_*`

---

## 6. Memory Coalescing Analysis

No dedicated "coalescing" metric section appears in the (truncated) content, but the following relevant material was found:

- **Sectors:** *"Aligned 32 byte-chunk of memory in a cache line or device memory. An L1 or L2 cache line is four sectors, i.e. 128 bytes."* Sector accesses classify as hits/misses based on tag/data presence.
- **Requests vs. wavefronts:** One memory instruction = 1 **request** (per warp) → accesses N **sectors** → processed in N **wavefronts** (1 wavefront/cycle through the L1TEX pipeline). Relationships: *requests:sectors is 1:N, wavefronts:sectors 1:N, requests:wavefronts 1:N*. Sectors/request reflects the **access pattern**; wavefronts reflect cycle cost.
- **Local memory coalescing:** *"local memory is arranged such that consecutive 32-bit words are accessed by consecutive thread IDs. Accesses are therefore fully coalesced as long as all threads in a warp access the same relative address."*
- **`lrc` unit:** The L2 Request Coalescer coalesces read requests before forwarding to L2.
- **Texture:** L1 is optimized for 2D spatial locality — nearby 2D accesses achieve optimal performance.

---

## 7. Shared Memory Bank Conflicts

**Bank model:** Shared memory has **32 banks**; successive 32-bit words map to successive banks. A 32-address request hitting 32 distinct banks is serviced simultaneously (32× bandwidth); two addresses in the same bank cause a **bank conflict** and serialization. No conflict occurs when threads access the same 32-bit word (reads are broadcast).

**Metric explicitly named in the doc (as a metrics-structure example):**
```
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum
```
with sub-metrics:
```
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.peak_sustained
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.peak_sustained_active
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.peak_sustained_active.per_second
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.peak_sustained_elapsed
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.peak_sustained_elapsed.per_second
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.per_cycle_active
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.per_cycle_elapsed
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.per_second
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.pct_of_peak_sustained_active
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed
```
Relevant unit/subunit decoders: `l1tex` (L1/Texture cache, with `t`/`m`/`d` stages), `lsu` (Load/Store unit), `shared` (shared memory subunit).

---

## 8. Guided Analysis Rules — ⚠️ Mostly Not Available

The provided (truncated) content contains only **one passing reference** to rules:

- Section **2.2.2** is titled *"Sections and Rules"* but only the sections table is shown
- *"A file named `.ncu-ignore` may be placed in any directory to have its contents ignored when the tool looks for section (and **rule**) files."*

No rule names, rule logic, or guided analysis workflow details appear in the truncated source.

---

## 9. Other Useful Metric Names Mentioned

| Metric | Type |
|---|---|
| `sm__inst_executed` | counter (roll-ups: `.sum`, `.avg`, `.min`, `.max`) |
| `smsp__average_warp_latency` | ratio (`.pct`, `.ratio`, `.max_rate`) |
| `sm__throughput` | throughput (`.pct_of_peak_sustained_active/elapsed`) |
| `gpu__time_duration` | workload duration metric |
| `device__attribute_sass_level` | attribute (not a SASS metric) |
| `unit__cycles_elapsed/active/stalled/idle` | cycle metric patterns |
| `breakdown:<throughput-metric>` | syntax to collect throughput breakdowns |

**Related sections also listed:** `SchedulerStats`, `WarpStateStats`, `SourceCounters`, `ComputeWorkloadAnalysis`, `InstructionStats`, `Nvlink*`, `PmSampling`, `Tile`, `WorkloadDistribution`.

**Duration caveat:** Nsight Compute measures kernel duration differently than Nsight Systems (clock locking, cache flushing between passes, serialization, semaphore-based timestamps). For comparable results, the doc recommends locking clocks externally with `nvidia-smi` and using `--clock-control none`, or `--replay-mode application --cache-control none` for cache-sensitive workloads.

# NVIDIA Nsight Compute CLI (`ncu`) — Usage Extraction

## Summary

This document is the official **Nsight Compute CLI User Guide (Chapter 5)**. It covers profiling workflows, kernel filtering, data collection options (`--set`, `--section`, `--metrics`), and output/report handling. **Important note upfront:** the specific section names you asked about (SpeedOfLight, MemoryWorkloadAnalysis, etc.) are **NOT enumerated in this document** — only `LaunchStats` and `Occupancy` appear (in a config-file example). The doc directs users to `--list-sections` / `--list-sets` to discover them. Details in the truncation note at the end.

---

## 1. Basic Profiling Command Examples

### Default profile (collects the `basic` set for all kernel launches)
```bash
$ ncu -o profile CuVectorAddMulti.exe
```
- Output is written to `profile.ncu-rep` (report file).
- Profiler output lines are prefixed with `==PROF==`.
- Kernels may be replayed multiple times (example shows "46 passes").

### Kernel selection / filtering options
| Option | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `-c`, `--launch-count` | Limit the number of profiled kernel launches |
| `-s`, `--launch-skip` | Skip N matching kernel launches before profiling (default: 0) |
| `--launch-skip-before-match` | Skip N launches counted regardless of kernel filters (default: 0) |
| `-k`, `--kernel-name` | Filter kernels by name (exact or `regex:`) |
| `--kernel-id` | Filter by `context-id:stream-id:[name-operator:]kernel-name:invocation-nr` |

**Exact examples from the doc:**
```bash
-k foo                     # exact match on kernel "foo"
-k regex:foo               # kernels containing "foo"
-k regex:"foo|bar"         # kernels containing "foo" or "bar"
--kernel-id ::foo:2        # 2nd invocation of kernel "foo"
--kernel-id :::".*5|3"     # 3rd invocation + all ending in "5"
--kernel-id ::regex:^.*foo$:    # kernels ending in "foo"
--kernel-id ::regex:'^(?!foo)': # all kernels EXCEPT those starting with "foo"
--kernel-id 1|5:2::7       # 7th invocation from context 1 or 5, stream 2
```
Related: `--kernel-name-base` accepts `function` (default), `demangled`, or `mangled`.

### Open report in UI
```bash
ncu-ui <MyReport.ncu-rep>
# or directly when profiling:
ncu --open-in-ui ...
```

---

## 2. Data Collection: `--set`, `--section`, `--metrics`

### `--set <set identifier>`
- Identifier of the section **set** to collect.
- **Default: `basic`** set is collected if no `--set` given.
- Full set: `--set full`
- If `--set` is not specified but `--section` or `--metrics` are used, **no sets** are collected.
- Use `--list-sets` to see available sets and the default.

### `--section <identifier>`
- Adds a section to collect:
  ```bash
  --section <section identifier>     # exact match
  --section "regex:.*Stats"          # regex matching full identifier (quote on bash)
  ```
- If no `--section` given → sections of the `basic` set are collected; if no sets found → all sections.
- Ignored with `--import` combined with `--page raw` or `--page source`.
- Can be passed multiple times.
- Example from config file section: `--section = LaunchStats, Occupancy`

### `--metrics <metric list>`
- Comma-separated list of individual metrics:
  ```bash
  --metrics sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed,<metric2>
  ```
- Supported **prefixes** (cannot be combined):
  | Prefix | Behavior |
  |---|---|
  | `regex:<expr>` | Expands to all metrics partially matching (use `^...$` for full match; no commas allowed in expression) |
  | `group:<name>` | All metrics of a metric group (not supported on `--import`) |
  | `breakdown:<metric>` | Expands to input metrics of a high-level throughput metric (not supported on `--import`) |
  | `pmsampling:<metric>` | Collect via PM sampling (single-pass, non-SASS-patched metrics only) |
- If a metric needs a suffix and no `regex:`/`group:` is used, it auto-expands to all first-level sub-metrics.
- If `--section` is also given, metrics from both are collected; otherwise only a temporary section with the listed metrics.

**Metric naming convention:** base name + suffix, e.g. `sm__throughput.avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed` (base = `sm__throughput`, suffix = `avg.pct_of_peak_sustained_elapsed`).

---

## 3. Listing Sections, Sets, Rules, and Metrics

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ncu --list-sets` | Lists all section sets + associated sections + estimated metric count (overhead estimate), then exits |
| `ncu --list-sections` | Lists all sections found in searched section folders, then exits |
| `ncu --list-rules` | Lists all rules found, then exits |
| `ncu --list-metrics` | Lists metrics collected from active sections (restricted by `--section` if given) |
| `ncu --list-chips` | Lists chips usable with `--chips` |

### Querying available metrics
```bash
ncu --query-metrics                          # query metrics for system devices
ncu --query-metrics --devices 0,2            # filter devices
ncu --query-metrics --chips tu102,gh100      # filter by chip
ncu --query-metrics-mode suffix --metrics <base metrics>   # get full names w/ suffixes
```
- **`--query-metrics-mode`**: `base` (default — base names only), `suffix` (all derived metrics for given bases; implies `--query-metrics`), `all` (full names of everything).
- **`--query-metrics-collection`** (default `profiling`): `device`, `groups`, `launch`, `numa`, `nvlink`, `occupancy`, `pmsampling`, `profiling`, `source`, `stats`, `warpsampling`.

---

## 4. Output / Report Options

### File options
| Option | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-o`, `--export <file>` | Write report to file; supports macros (below). If set without `--page`, nothing prints to console | temp file, deleted after |
| `-f`, `--force-overwrite` | Overwrite existing output files | off (errors instead) |
| `-i`, `--import <file>` | Import a saved report (most other options unavailable; filter options marked [1] still work) | — |
| `--open-in-ui` | Open report in UI instead of terminal (host platforms only) | — |
| `--log-file <file>` | Tool output to file, or `stdout` / `stderr` | console |

**Filtered export** (export a subset from one report to another):
```bash
ncu --import Old.ncu-rep --export New.ncu-rep [filter options]
```
(`--metrics` and `--section` are NOT supported for filtered export.)

### Console output options
| Option | Values | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `--page` | `details`, `raw`, `source`, `session` | `details` (nothing printed if `--export` set without `--page`) |
| `--csv` | comma-separated output; implies `--print-units base` | off |
| `--print-source` | `sass`, `ptx`, `tileir`, `cuda`, `cuda,sass`, `cuda,tileir`, `tileir,ptx`, `tileir,sass` | `sass` |
| `--print-details` | `header`, `body`, `all` (replaces deprecated `--details-all`) | `header` |
| `--print-units` | `auto`, `base` | `auto` |
| `--print-metric-name` | `label`, `name`, `label-name` | `label` |
| `--print-summary` | `none`, `per-gpu`, `per-kernel`, `per-nvtx` | `none` |
| `--print-metric-instances` | `none`, `values`, `details` | `none` |
| `--print-kernel-base` | function/demangled/mangled basis for output names | `demangled` |
| `--print-fp` | numeric metrics as floating point | `false` |
| `--print-rule-details` | extra rule result details (no effect in CSV) | `false` |
| `--print-nvtx-rename` | `none`, `kernel` | `none` |
| `--print-metric-attribution` | attribution level for Green Context results | `false` |

### File name macros (for `-o`/`--export`)
| Macro | Expands to |
|---|---|
| `%h` | Hostname |
| `%q{ENV_NAME}` | Environment variable content, e.g. `report_%q{OMPI_COMM_WORLD_RANK}` |
| `%p` | Process ID of ncu |
| `%i` | Lowest unused integer (unique filename; usable once) |
| `%%` | Literal `%` (usable in path) |

### MPI / multi-process examples
```bash
# All ranks, single report:
ncu --target-processes all -o <report-name> mpirun [mpi args] <app> [app args]

# Multi-node, unique report per rank:
mpirun [mpi args] ncu -o report_%q{OMPI_COMM_WORLD_RANK} <app> [app args]

# TCP communicator:
mpirun [mpi args] ncu --communicator=tcp --communicator-num-peers=<ranks> -o report <app>
```

---

## 5. Other Useful Options Mentioned

- **Replay**: `--replay-mode kernel|application|range|app-range` (default `kernel`)
- **Cache/clock control**: `--cache-control all|none` (default `all`); `--clock-control base|boost|force-boost|none|reset` (default `boost`)
- **Kill after count**: `--kill on|off` (default `no`) — terminate app once `--launch-count` reached
- **Profile from start**: `--profile-from-start on|off` (default `yes`)
- **Config file**: `config.ncu-cfg`, INI-style, searched in CWD, `$HOME/.config/NVIDIA Corporation` (Linux), `%APPDATA%\NVIDIA Corporation\` (Windows); override with `--config-file-path`; disable with `--config-file off`
- **Response files**: `ncu @FileName ...`

---

## ⚠️ Truncation / Completeness Notes

1. **Specific section names NOT listed**: This CLI guide does **not** enumerate `SpeedOfLight`, `MemoryWorkloadAnalysis`, `SchedulerStats`, or `WarpStateStats`. Only **`LaunchStats`** and **`Occupancy`** appear (in a config-file sample: `--section = LaunchStats, Occupancy`). The document explicitly defers to `ncu --list-sections` / `ncu --list-sets` and the separate **Profiling Guide** ("Sets and Sections" chapter) for the full catalog. To verify those sections on your system, run:
   ```bash
   ncu --list-sections
   ncu --section SpeedOfLight --section MemoryWorkloadAnalysis -o profile ./app
   ```
2. **Nvprof Transition Guide (§5.6)** is effectively truncated — it only says "Refer to the older documentation" with a link to the Archives.
3. One minor doc inconsistency: the text says results are "written by default to `profile.nsight-cuprof`" but the example output shows `profile.ncu-rep` — **`.ncu-rep` is the current extension**.
4. The command-line option tables themselves (General, Launch, Attach, Profile, PM/Warp Sampling, File, Console Output, MPS) appear complete in this capture, including defaults.

# Extraction from CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide

**⚠️ Truncation Notice:** The provided content is **truncated mid-way through Section 10.2.3.2** ("Shared Memory in Matrix Multiplication (C=AB)"). This has the following impact on your request:

| Requested Topic | Availability |
|---|---|
| (1) Coalesced global memory access | ✅ **Fully available** |
| (2) Shared memory bank conflicts | ⚠️ **Partially available** (theory yes; padding examples truncated) |
| (3) Occupancy (Calculator, `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor`, `__launch_bounds__`) | ❌ **Not present** (section truncated) |
| (4) Memory-bound kernel guidance | ⚠️ **Partially available** (bandwidth metrics & transfer guidance yes; dedicated later sections truncated) |

The truncation point is: *"[Using shared memory to improve the global memory load efficiency in matrix multiplication]"* — the content ends immediately after the `coalescedMultiply` kernel listing.

---

## 1. Coalesced Global Memory Access (Section 10.2.1) ✅

### Core Recommendation

> **High Priority:** Ensure global memory accesses are coalesced whenever possible.

**Definition:** "Global memory loads and stores by threads of a warp are coalesced by the device into as few as possible transactions."

### Coalescing Rules by Compute Capability

- **Compute capability 6.0 or higher:** "The concurrent accesses of the threads of a warp will coalesce into a number of transactions equal to the number of **32-byte transactions** necessary to service all of the threads of the warp."
- **Certain devices of compute capability 5.2:** L1-caching of global memory accesses can be optionally enabled; if enabled, "the number of required transactions is equal to the number of required **128-byte aligned segments**."
- **Compute capability 6.0+:** "L1-caching is the default, however the data access unit is **32-byte** regardless of whether global loads are cached in L1 or not."
- **GDDR memory + ECC:** "On devices with GDDR memory, accessing memory in a coalesced way is even more important when ECC is turned on. Scattered accesses increase ECC memory transfer overhead, especially when writing data to global memory."

### Simple (Ideal) Access Pattern — Section 10.2.1.1

> "The *k*-th thread accesses the *k*-th word in a 32-byte aligned array. Not all threads need to participate."

- Warp accessing adjacent 4-byte words (e.g., `float`) → **four coalesced 32-byte transactions**.
- If only a subset of words in a segment is requested, "the full segment is fetched anyway."
- Permuted accesses within/across the four segments still result in only four 32-byte transactions (CC 6.0+).

### Misaligned Access — Section 10.2.1.2

> "If sequential threads in a warp access memory that is sequential but not aligned with a 32-byte segment, **five 32-byte segments** will be requested."

**Alignment guidance:**
> "Memory allocated through the CUDA Runtime API, such as via `cudaMalloc()`, is guaranteed to be aligned to at least **256 bytes**. Therefore, choosing sensible thread block sizes, such as **multiples of the warp size (i.e., 32 on current GPUs)**, facilitates memory accesses by warps that are properly aligned."

### Misalignment Effects — `offsetCopy` Kernel (Section 10.2.1.3)

Exact code snippet:

```cpp
__global__ void offsetCopy(float *odata, float* idata, int offset)
{
    int xid = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x + offset;
    odata[xid] = idata[xid];
}
```

Measured results on **NVIDIA Tesla V100 (compute capability 7.0)**, offset varied 0–32:

- **No offset or offsets that are multiples of 8 words:** four 32-byte transactions → achieved bandwidth **≈ 790 GB/s**.
- **Otherwise:** five 32-byte segments loaded per warp; naively expected ~4/5 of throughput, but measured **≈ 9/10**, "because adjacent warps reuse the cache lines their neighbors fetched."

### Strided Accesses — `strideCopy` Kernel (Section 10.2.1.4)

Exact code snippet:

```cpp
__global__ void strideCopy(float *odata, float* idata, int stride)
{
    int xid = (blockIdx.x*blockDim.x + threadIdx.x)*stride;
    odata[xid] = idata[xid];
}
```

Effects on Tesla V100 (CC 7.0):

- **Stride 2:** "leads to a load of **eight L2 cache segments per warp**" → "a 50% of load/store efficiency since half the elements in the transaction are not used and represent wasted bandwidth."
- **Increasing stride:** "the effective bandwidth decreases until the point where **32 32-byte segments are loaded for the 32 threads** in a warp."

> "Non-unit-stride global memory accesses should be avoided whenever possible. One method for doing so utilizes **shared memory**."

---

## 2. Shared Memory Bank Conflicts (Section 10.2.3.1) ⚠️ Partial

### Available Explanation

> "Because it is on-chip, shared memory has much higher bandwidth and lower latency than local and global memory — **provided there are no bank conflicts between the threads**."

**Bank structure:**
> "To achieve high memory bandwidth for concurrent accesses, shared memory is divided into equally sized memory modules (*banks*) that can be accessed simultaneously. Therefore, any memory load or store of *n* addresses that spans *n* distinct memory banks can be serviced simultaneously, yielding an effective bandwidth that is *n* times as high as the bandwidth of a single bank."

**Conflict serialization:**
> "However, if multiple addresses of a memory request map to the same memory bank, the accesses are **serialized**. The hardware splits a memory request that has bank conflicts into as many separate conflict-free requests as necessary, decreasing the effective bandwidth by a factor equal to the number of separate memory requests."

**Broadcast exception:**
> "The one exception here is when multiple threads in a warp address the **same** shared memory location, resulting in a **broadcast**. In this case, multiple broadcasts from different banks are coalesced into a single **multicast** from the requested shared memory locations to the threads."

**Bank mapping (CC 5.x and newer):**
> "On devices of compute capability 5.x or newer, each bank has a bandwidth of **32 bits every clock cycle**, and successive 32-bit words are assigned to successive banks. The warp size is 32 threads and the number of banks is also **32**, so bank conflicts can occur between any threads in the warp."

**No penalty for non-sequential shared access:**
> "Aside from memory bank conflicts, there is **no penalty for non-sequential or unaligned accesses** by a warp in shared memory."

### Related Available Example: Shared Memory Tiling (Section 10.2.3.2)

The unoptimized kernel (effective bandwidth **119.9 GB/s** on Tesla V100):

```cpp
__global__ void simpleMultiply(float *a, float* b, float *c,
                               int N)
{
    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    float sum = 0.0f;
    for (int i = 0; i < TILE_DIM; i++) {
        sum += a[row*TILE_DIM+i] * b[i*N+col];
    }
    c[row*N+col] = sum;
}
```

The shared-memory version (`__syncwarp()` after tile load):

```cpp
__global__ void coalescedMultiply(float *a, float* b, float *c,
                                  int N)
{
    __shared__ float aTile[TILE_DIM][TILE_DIM];

    int row = blockIdx.y * blockDim.y + threadIdx.y;
    int col = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
    float sum = 0.0f;
    aTile[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = a[row*TILE_DIM+threadIdx.x];
    __syncwarp();
    for (int i = 0; i < TILE_DIM; i++) {
        sum += aTile[threadIdx.y][i]* b[i*N+col];
    }
    c[row*N+col] = sum;
}
```

### ❌ Truncated Content

- **Padding techniques** — the classic padding example lives in **Section 10.2.3.3 "Shared Memory in Matrix Multiplication (C=AAᵀ)"**, which is **not included** in the provided content (the table of contents references it, but the body was cut off).
- **Section 10.2.3.4 "Asynchronous Copy from Global Memory to Shared Memory"** — also truncated.

---

## 3. Occupancy ❌ Not Present in Provided Content

The following requested topics appear **nowhere** in the supplied text — they occur in later chapters of the full guide (Execution Configuration Optimizations) that were truncated:

- **CUDA Occupancy Calculator**
- **`cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` API**
- **`__launch_bounds__` qualifier**
- **Register/shared-memory per-block limits and their effect on occupancy**

I will not reproduce these from memory, since you asked for exact snippets from the document. **To obtain them, provide the guide's sections from ~Section 10.3 onward** (in the full guide, look for "Thread and Block Heuristics," "Occupancy," and "Effects of Shared Memory" subsections).

---

## 4. Memory-Bound Kernel Guidance ⚠️ Partial

The following guidance relevant to memory-bound kernels **is** available:

### Bandwidth as Primary Metric (Section 9.2)

> "Bandwidth — the rate at which data can be transferred — is one of the most important gating factors for performance. Almost all changes to code should be made in the context of how they affect bandwidth."

> **High Priority:** Use the effective bandwidth of your computation as a metric when measuring performance and optimization benefits.

**Theoretical bandwidth example (Tesla V100):** HBM2, 877 MHz memory clock, 4096-bit interface:

```
(0.877×10⁹ × (4096/8) × 2) ÷ 10⁹ = 898 GB/s
```

**Effective bandwidth formula (exact parameter names):**

```
Effective bandwidth = ((Br + Bw) ÷ 10⁹) ÷ time
```

where `Br` = bytes read per kernel, `Bw` = bytes written per kernel, `time` in seconds. Example for a 2048×2048 float matrix copy:

```
Effective bandwidth = ((2048² × 4 × 2) ÷ 10⁹) ÷ time
```

**ECC caveat:** "On GPUs with GDDR memory with ECC enabled the available DRAM is reduced by 6.25%... Fetching ECC bits... reduced the effective bandwidth by approximately 20%... HBM2 memories, on the other hand, provide dedicated ECC resources, allowing overhead-free ECC protection."

**Visual Profiler throughput metrics (exact names):** `Requested Global Load Throughput`, `Requested Global Store Throughput`, `Global Load Throughput`, `Global Store Throughput`, `DRAM Read Throughput`, `DRAM Write Throughput`. Comparing requested vs. actual bandwidth estimates "how much bandwidth is wasted by suboptimal coalescing."

### Arithmetic Intensity / Data Transfer Minimization (Sections 3.2, 10.1)

> **High Priority:** Minimize data transfer between the host and the device, even if it means running some kernels on the device that do not show performance gains when compared with running them on the host CPU.

- Bandwidth asymmetry: **898 GB/s** device-to-GPU (V100) vs. **16 GB/s** host-to-device (PCIe x16 Gen3).
- Operations-per-element ratio: matrix addition is **O(1)** (N² ops vs. 3N² elements transferred → poor GPU candidate); matrix multiplication is **O(N)** (N³ ops → benefit grows with size).
- "Data should be kept on the device as long as possible"; "Intermediate data structures should be created in device memory, operated on by the device, and destroyed without ever being mapped by the host."
- "Batching many small transfers into one larger transfer performs significantly better."
- **Pinned memory:** "On PCIe x16 Gen3 cards, for example, pinned memory can attain roughly **12 GB/s**" — allocated via `cudaHostAlloc()`; pre-existing memory pinned via `cudaHostRegister()`. Warning: "Pinned memory should not be overused... a scarce resource."

### L2 Cache Persistence Controls (Section 10.2.2, CC 8.0+)

Relevant for memory-bound kernels with repeated data access. Exact snippets:

```cpp
cudaGetDeviceProperties(&prop, device_id);
cudaDeviceSetLimit(cudaLimitPersistingL2CacheSize, prop.persistingL2CacheMaxSize);
```

```cpp
cudaStreamAttrValue stream_attribute;
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.base_ptr  = reinterpret_cast<void*>(ptr);
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.num_bytes = num_bytes;                    // Must be less than cudaDeviceProp::accessPolicyMaxWindowSize
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.hitRatio  = 1.0;
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.hitProp   = cudaAccessPropertyPersisting;
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.missProp  = cudaAccessPropertyStreaming;
cudaStreamSetAttribute(stream, cudaStreamAttributeAccessPolicyWindow, &stream_attribute);
```

Tuned version to avoid thrashing (when persistent data > set-aside L2):

```cpp
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.base_ptr  = reinterpret_cast<void*>(data_persistent);
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.num_bytes = 20*1024*1024;                                  // 20 MB
stream_attribute.accessPolicyWindow.hitRatio  = (20*1024*1024)/((float)freqSize*sizeof(int));
```

Result: up to **50% performance increase** when persistent data fits the 30 MB set-aside (A100 has 40 MB total L2); ~10% drop from thrashing if untuned and oversized.

### ❌ Truncated

Dedicated guidance specifically labeled for memory-bound kernels (e.g., minimizing instructions in bandwidth-limited kernels, "Maximize Memory Throughput" subsections) appears later in the guide and was **not included**.

---

## Summary

- **Fully extractable:** Coalescing rules, `offsetCopy`/`strideCopy` kernels, misalignment/stride performance data, bank conflict theory with broadcast exception, bandwidth formulas, pinned memory, L2 access policy window APIs.
- **Missing due to truncation:** All occupancy content (`__launch_bounds__`, `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor`, Occupancy Calculator), the padding example for bank conflicts (Section 10.2.3.3), and async-copy shared memory content (10.2.3.4). Re-submit content from Section 10.2.3.3 through the execution-configuration chapter to complete the extraction.

**Summary:** The provided content covers Nsight Compute release notes from **2026.3.1 (latest)** back to **2019.4**. The newest/current version is **2026.3.1**. Below is the extracted GPU architecture, OS, and CUDA toolkit support information. **Note: The content is truncated** — the "Supported Platforms/GPUs" and "Known Issues" sections referenced in the page intro are *not* included, and the document cuts off mid-history at 2019.4 (details at the end).

## 1. Latest Version

| Last major feature release | 2026.3 (Rubin architecture support, CUDA 13.4, Tile IR view, Compute Triage Guide) |

**标题**: CUDA Programming Guide — CUDA Programming Guide

Back to top

# CUDA Programming Guide[#](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/index.html#cuda-programming-guide "Link to this heading")

**CUDA and the CUDA Programming Guide**

CUDA is a parallel computing platform and programming model developed by NVIDIA that enables dramatic increases in computing performance by harnessing the power of the GPU. It allows developers to accelerate compute-intensive applications and is widely used in fields such as deep learning, scientific computing, and high-performance computing (HPC).

This CUDA Programming Guide is the official, comprehensive resource on the CUDA programming model and how to write code that executes on the GPU using the CUDA platform. This guide covers everything from the CUDA programming model and the CUDA platform to the details of language extensions and covers how to make use of specific hardware and software features. This guide provides a pathway for developers to learn CUDA if they are new, and also provides an essential resource for developers as they build applications using CUDA.

**Organization of This Guide**

Even for developers who primarily use libraries, frameworks, or DSLs, an understanding of the CUDA programming model and how GPUs execute code is valuable in knowing what is happening behind the layers of abstraction. This guide starts with a chapter on the [CUDA programming model](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/01-introduction/programming-model.html#programming-model) outside of any specific programming language which is applicable to anyone interested in understanding how CUDA works, even non-developers.

The guide is broken down into five primary parts:

- Part 1: Introduction and Programming Model Abstract
  
  - A language agnostic overview of the CUDA programming model as well as a brief tour of the CUDA platform.
  - This section is meant to be read by anyone wanting to understand GPUs and the concepts of executing code on GPUs, even if they are not developers.
- Part 2: Programming GPUs in CUDA
  
  - The basics of programming GPUs in C++ and Python.
  - This section is meant to be read by anyone wanting to get started in GPU programming.
  - This section is meant to be instructional, not complete, and teaches the most important and common parts of CUDA programming, including some common performance considerations.
- Part 3: Advanced CUDA
  
  - Introduces some more advance features of CUDA that enable both fine-grained control and more opportunities to maximize performance, including the use of multiple GPUs in a single application.
  - This section concludes with a [tour of the features covered in part 4](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-programming-guide/03-advanced/feature-survey.html#tour-of-features) with a brief introduction to the purpose and function of each, sorted by when and why a developer may find each feature useful.
- Part 4: CUDA Features

<answer>

## 1. 用 Nsight Compute 分析（采集 → 定位瓶颈）

**采集命令**（来源：Nsight Compute CLI User Guide）

```bash
# 默认 basic 集合（含 LaunchStats/Occupancy 静态数据）
ncu -o profile ./myapp

# 完整采集（含 MemoryWorkloadAnalysis、WarpStateStats、SourceCounters 等，需多次 replay）
ncu --set full -o profile_full ./myapp

# 精准采集：只取需要的 section
ncu --section SpeedOfLight --section MemoryWorkloadAnalysis --section Occupancy \
    -k regex:my_kernel -c 1 -o profile_mem ./myapp

# 查看可用集合/section/metrics
ncu --list-sets
ncu --list-sections
ncu --query-metrics --devices 0
```

- `-k regex:...` 按 kernel 名过滤；`-c/--launch-count` 限制 launch 次数；`-s/--launch-skip` 跳过前 N 次。
- 打开报告：`ncu-ui profile.ncu-rep`，或采集时加 `--open-in-ui`。
- 计时与 Nsight Systems 不可直接比：ncu 默认锁时钟 + flush cache；要可比可加 `--clock-control none --cache-control none` 或外部用 `nvidia-smi` 锁频。

**判读顺序**（来源：Nsight Compute Profiling Guide）

1. **SpeedOfLight**：对比 Compute (SM) 与 Memory throughput。Memory 接近理论峰值、SM 低 → 访存受限。
2. **MemoryWorkloadAnalysis**（官方描述：当 Mem Busy 打满、Max Bandwidth 耗尽、或 Mem Pipes Busy 达到发射上限时内存成为瓶颈）：
   - 看 L1/L2 命中率、DRAM 读写量；
   - 关键概念：**1 条访存指令 = 1 request（每 warp）→ 访问 N 个 sector（32 字节对齐块）→ N 个 wavefront（每 cycle 1 个）**。sectors/request 高 = 访存模式差（未合并）。
   - 理想情况：warp 内线程连续访问连续 32 字节 sector，1 request 只需 4 sectors（128B cache line）。
3. **Occupancy**：对比 Theoretical vs Achieved Occupancy；官方明确指出 occupancy 受 threads / registers / shared memory / barriers 限制，且 "higher occupancy does not always result in higher performance"，但低 occupancy 会降低延迟隐藏能力。`launch__occupancy_per_*` 指标即由 CUDA Occupancy Calculator 逻辑计算。
4. **WarpStateStats / SchedulerStats**：看 stall 原因（如 `long_scoreboard` 表示等全局内存返回）。

## 2. Memory coalescing 优化

（来源：CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide §10.2.1）

- 原则："Ensure global memory accesses are coalesced whenever possible"（High Priority）。CC ≥ 6.0：warp 的并发访问合并为所需的最少 32 字节事务数。
- 理想模式：第 k 个线程访问 32 字节对齐数组的第 k 个字；块大小取 warp 大小（32）的倍数以利对齐；`cudaMalloc` 保证 ≥256 字节对齐。
- 反面教材（官方实测，Tesla V100）：
  - 错位访问（offset 非 8 字倍数）→ 每 warp 5 个 32B 段而非 4 个；
  - 步长访问 stride=2 → 每 warp 8 个 L2 段，50% 效率浪费；stride 大到每线程落独立段时，1 warp 需 32 个段。
  - "Non-unit-stride global memory accesses should be avoided whenever possible" — 可借助 shared memory 中转。
- 常见改法：AoS → SoA；交换循环/线程映射让 `threadIdx.x` 对应连续地址；错位时调整起始偏移。
- ncu 侧验证：对比优化前后 MemoryWorkloadAnalysis 中 L1/L2 sectors/request 及 DRAM 传输量是否下降。

## 3. Shared memory 与 bank conflict

（来源：Profiling Guide + Best Practices §10.2.3）

**bank 模型（CC 5.x+）**：shared memory 分 **32 个 bank**，连续 32-bit 字映射到连续 bank；warp 32 线程访问 32 个不同 bank 可并行服务；多地址落同一 bank（不同字）→ 串行化，带宽按冲突数下降；**例外**：多线程读**同一**字 → broadcast/multicast，无冲突。非顺序/非对齐 shared 访问本身无惩罚（只看 bank 冲突）。

**ncu 检测指标**：
```
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum
# 或按比率看：
l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu.sum.pct_of_peak_sustained_active
```
查询当前架构可用指标：
```bash
ncu --query-metrics-mode suffix --metrics l1tex__data_bank_conflicts_pipe_lsu --devices 0
```

**消除方法**：tile 加 padding（如 `__shared__ float tile[TILE_DIM][TILE_DIM+1]`）错开列访问的 bank；调整数据布局/访问映射。

**shared memory 用于合并访存**（官方矩阵乘 tile 示例，Best Practices §10.2.3.2）：
```cpp
__shared__ float aTile[TILE_DIM][TILE_DIM];
aTile[threadIdx.y][threadIdx.x] = a[row*TILE_DIM+threadIdx.x];
__syncwarp();   // 块内 >1 warp 时用 __syncthreads()
```
注：官方 padding 完整示例（§10.2.3.3）本轮抓取被截断，padding 写法属常见做法但本轮未取得官方原文。

## 4. Occupancy 计算与提升

（来源：Profiling Guide Occupancy section；API 部分为先验知识、本轮未从官方原文核实）

- ncu 的 Occupancy section 直接给出 Theoretical/Achieved occupancy 及限制因素表，无需手工算；
- 手工/API 途径（先验知识，未核实）：`cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor(&numBlocks, kernel, blockSize, dynamicSmem)`；CUDA 附带 Occupancy Calculator 表格；`__launch_bounds__(maxThreadsPerBlock, minBlocksPerMultiprocessor)` 约束寄存器分配。
- 提升手段：减小每线程寄存器（`__launch_bounds__`）、减少每块 shared memory、block size 取 128–256（warp 整数倍）、必要时用 carveout 增大 L1 vs shared 配比（`cudaFuncAttributePreferredSharedMemoryCarveout`）。
- 注意官方提醒：occupancy 高≠性能好；访存受限 kernel 更关键是足够的并发访存（sector 流水线打满）和减少无效传输。

## 5. 版本适用性（Nsight Compute ↔ 目标 GPU）

（来源：Nsight Compute Release Notes，docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ReleaseNotes）

| 目标 GPU 架构 | 需要 Nsight Compute ≥ |
|---|---|
| Ampere (GA100/SM 8.x) | 2020.1 |
| Ada | 2022.3 |
| Hopper (GH100) | 2022.3 |
| Blackwell | 2024.4（2025.3 起改进，2026.2 补齐部分消费 SKU） |
| Rubin | 2026.3 |

当前最新版 2026.3.1。建议直接用 CUDA Toolkit 自带 ncu（如 2026.3 ↔ CUDA 13.4，2022.3 ↔ CUDA 11.8），版本即随 toolkit 锁定。⚠️ 官方"Supported platforms/GPUs 完整列表"一节本轮抓取被截断，上表是从各版本 release note 条目合并得出的，非单一官方对照表。

## 来源

- https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ProfilingGuide/index.html （正文取得，但在 §2.4.2 处被工具明确截断；guided rules 细节未取到）
- https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/NsightComputeCli/index.html （正文取得，Nvprof 迁移节截断）
- https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-best-practices-guide/index.html （正文取得，§10.2.3.2 处截断；occupancy 章节未取得）
- https://docs.nvidia.com/nsight-compute/ReleaseNotes/index.html （正文取得，Supported platforms 节缺失）

**未核实/受阻处**：(1) `cudaOccupancyMaxActiveBlocksPerMultiprocessor` 与 `__launch_bounds__` 的精确签名本轮未取到官方原文（新版 CUDA 编程指南站点改版，旧 anchor URL 404）；(2) bank conflict padding 官方示例被截断；(3) 完整支持 GPU 矩阵表被截断，上表为 release note 合并推断。
